title: Richmond's streetcar system at its height, 1925
method: Today's buildings are dated by OSM start_date or the City of Richmond's recorded year built; buildings since lost downtown come from the 1924–25 Sanborn tracing. The car lines are placed on today's OpenStreetMap streets, following Harland Bartholomew & Associates' plate 'Early Transit Routes, 1888 & 1925' (City Planning Commission, 1943). Curated outlines are placed from today's street intersections and published descriptions; they are not surveyed. Era rules match OSM names, refs and tags; the first match wins.
about: Richmond opened the first practical electric streetcar system in 1888; by the 1920s it reached the suburbs it had created, from Westhampton to Fulton and from Lakeside to Forest Hill Park.

epochs.title: The streetcar city
epochs.note: Car lines as Harland Bartholomew & Associates mapped them for 1925: within the city limits of the day, with the Lakeside and Westhampton lines running on beyond.

atGrade.note: Fifth and Seventh streets cross East Leigh Street on bridges built in 1971; before them the streets are drawn meeting at grade (approximate).

Campus Drive past the Burying Ground: the road built through here in 1912 and widened in 1947 ran on the ground; no source found dates today's bridge, so before 1950 the drive and the Westhampton cars are drawn at grade (approximate).

Chamberlayne Avenue's bridges over the railroad north of Leigh Street were built in 1992 (twin one-way decks, a ramp and their walkways); what crossed there in 1925 is not known here, so before 1992 the avenue is drawn crossing at grade (approximate).

features.name: Marshall Street Viaduct
features.note: Opened 12 February 1911 by the Richmond and Henrico Railway from College Street, at the east edge of the medical college, across Shockoe Valley to 21st Street at Jefferson Park, with tracks for the streetcars; closed by the city in 1970 and taken down. Drawn straight on the car line between those ends: its exact line, length and height are approximate.

features.name: Free Bridge (Ninth Street)
features.note: The low iron bridge from Ninth Street to Manchester, toll-free, built 1878 and closed after the floods of 1969 and 1972, when the Manchester Bridge replaced it. The Forest Hill cars crossed on it. Drawn on the line of today's Manchester Bridge, where the car line is placed, its deck 4 m above the river; south of it the cars run on in the street to Semmes Avenue. Its exact line and height are approximate.

features.name: Richmond–Ashland viaduct
features.note: The interurban's half-mile concrete viaduct, from the second floor of its terminal at 814 West Broad Street north over the Seaboard's tracks to just south of Brook Road. Drawn straight between the terminal and the point where the line meets Brook Road's side: its line and height are approximate.

features.name: The Boulevard over the RF&P (before 1943)
features.note: The Boulevard's bridge over the RF&P by the fair grounds dates from 1943; what carried the street and the fair grounds spur across the tracks before it is not known here. Today's ground has the tracks in a cut, so the street and the spur are drawn across it on one plain low deck on the line of the spur, from the fair's revival in 1906: its form, length and height are approximate.

features.name: Virginia State Fair Grounds
features.note: The State Fair grounds at the tip of the triangle between the Boulevard and Hermitage Road, from the revived fair of 1906 until the fair moved out in 1941; The Diamond stands there now. Outline follows the two roads, after the 1925 Sanborn sheet 468; the south edge is approximate.

features.name: Virginia State Fair Grounds
features.note: The fair grounds, 9 m inside the roads around them: while the fair stood here, today's streets, lots and buildings on the site are not drawn.

features.name: Fair Grounds mile track
features.note: The fair's one-mile racetrack, its south turn traced from the 1925 Sanborn sheet 468 (marked 'One Mile Track'), its straights run parallel to the Boulevard; the north turn, off the sheet, is drawn to make up the mile and is approximate.

features.name: Richmond and Petersburg (Atlantic Coast Line) approach to Byrd Street Station
features.note: The track from the north end of the Richmond and Petersburg bridge (OSM w710689016) across the Haxall Canal into Byrd Street Station at Seventh and Byrd Streets, the R&P's original Richmond station and later the Atlantic Coast Line's headquarters, closed in 1958. Today nothing of it is mapped north of the bridge. Approximate: one track along the middle of the station's throat, read by eye from the USGS 1:24,000 Richmond quadrangles of 1934 and 1956 (which show the line crossing the canal and fanning into the station yard between Seventh and Eighth Streets south of Byrd) and joined to the bridge's mapped end, about 20 m east of where the maps put it. Drawn with the bridge, 1902 to 1970; the years are the bridge's, not the track's.

features.name: Richmond and Petersburg (Atlantic Coast Line) approach in Manchester
features.note: The track from the south end of the Richmond and Petersburg bridge (OSM w710689016): along the old grade OSM maps as a path today (w1065955897), then on to the Southern's line beside it, so the bridge lands on track, not on the hillside. Approximate: where the R&P met the Southern here is not drawn from a source. Drawn with the bridge, 1902 to 1970.

features.name: Chesapeake and Ohio approach to the Church Hill Tunnel
features.note: The C&O's line to the Church Hill Tunnel's west portal, by 18th Street just north of Marshall: it left the old Virginia Central line west of 17th Street and curved southeast. The tunnel opened in 1873, collapsed on October 2, 1925, and its western end was sealed the following spring, so it is drawn through 1925 and not after. Its course: OSM's abandoned branch (w169784705) from the junction with today's Peninsula Subdivision south to 17th Street; then the C&O spur shown on the 1924–25 Sanborn map, volume 1, sheet 24, crossing the block between 17th and 18th Streets, Marshall and Clay, between the Richmond Cold Storage and International Harvester warehouses (the sheet fitted to the four corners of the block, to about a meter, and the line set midway between the warehouses standing today); then straight across 18th Street to the portal mapped in OSM (the tunnel, w6036486). Approximate.

features.name: Westhampton line
features.note: West on Floyd Avenue from Robinson Street to the belt line railroad, under it in a tunnel, then a little north to Grove Avenue; out Grove to Three Chopt Road; then on its own right-of-way beside Three Chopt to Towana Road, and on (the line of today's Campus Drive) to Westhampton Park, which became the University of Richmond's campus in 1914. The right-of-way beside Three Chopt is drawn along the road itself.

features.name: Belmont line
features.route: Broad Street – Sheppard Street – Cary Street – Belmont Avenue
features.note: The Broad Street line's extension west from Robinson Street to Sheppard, south to Cary, later carried on eleven blocks to Garrett Street. Which street carried the last stretch is read from the 1925 plate's 'Belmont' label.

features.name: Broad Street line
features.route: Broad Street, Sheppard Street to Church Hill
features.note: Broad Street, the spine of the system, from the Belmont line's turn at Sheppard Street east to Church Hill. The east end is approximate.

features.name: State Fair Grounds spur
features.route: Boulevard north to the Fair Grounds
features.note: The 1925 plate shows a short spur north from Broad Street ending in a loop. It is drawn here up the Boulevard to the State Fair Grounds (1906–1941, on the site of The Diamond); which street the spur took is not certain.

features.name: Main Street line
features.route: Main Street, Robinson Street to Shockoe
features.note: West Main Street, which the line turned into a commercial street through the Fan, east to Shockoe. The west end is approximate.

features.name: Harrison Street line
features.note: A crosstown link on Harrison Street between the Main, Floyd and Broad lines, as the 1925 plate shows it.

features.name: Reservoir (Byrd) Park line
features.note: Down Robinson Street to Reservoir Park (Byrd Park), one of the trolley's favorite destinations, along Lakeview Avenue as the 1925 plate labels it. Lakeview Avenue is mapped today only to Shields Lake; the last 450 m, to the end of the line, are drawn straight and are approximate.

features.name: Clay Street line
features.note: Sprague's first line of 1888 ran from Church Hill to Clay and Hancock Streets; the 1925 plate still shows Clay Street. The ends are approximate.

features.name: Brookland and Lakeside line
features.route: 1st Street – North Avenue – Brookland Park – Chamberlayne – Laburnum – Hermitage Road
features.note: Over the First Street viaduct (1891) into Barton Heights, then west along Brookland Park Boulevard, north up the median of Chamberlayne Avenue, west on Laburnum and north on Hermitage Road to Lakeside Park and Lewis Ginter's Lakeside Wheel Club. The run beyond Hermitage Road along Lakeside Avenue is approximate. OSM maps Monteiro Street with a gap north of Lakewood Street; the line is drawn straight across it.

features.name: Highland Park line
features.route: 5th Street – Northside Viaduct – Highland Park loop
features.note: North on Fifth Street over the Northside Viaduct (opened in 1891, an iron bridge 1,200 feet long) to Chestnut Hill and Highland Park, and after 1908 round a loop by Meadowbridge Road, Milton Street and Highland Street (the cross street joining them, Second Avenue here, is approximate). The Hull Street–Highland Park line was Richmond's last: the last car ran on 25 November 1949. Fifth Street is drawn straight across today's interstate, as it ran then.

features.name: Marshall Street line (Fulton)
features.route: Marshall Street Viaduct – Church Hill – Fulton
features.note: Across Shockoe Valley on the Marshall Street Viaduct (1911, since demolished: drawn straight) from College Street to 21st Street at Jefferson Park, out Marshall Street, and down to Fulton along Williamsburg Avenue. The route from Marshall Street down to Fulton is approximate.

features.name: Venable Street line
features.route: 17th Street – Venable Street – 25th Street – Nine Mile Road
features.note: North on 17th Street, east along Venable Street through Union Hill, and up 25th Street to Nine Mile Road, the road the Seven Pines line took out of the city (chartered along 25th to 29th Streets and Nine Mile Road). The federal government bought the Seven Pines line in 1918 for a wartime plant; how far cars ran out Nine Mile Road in 1925 is not certain.

features.name: Jefferson Avenue line
features.note: Up 21st Street and out Jefferson Avenue past Jefferson Park, one of the trolley's pleasure grounds, as the 1925 plate shows it.

features.name: Hull Street line
features.note: Over the Mayo Bridge into Manchester and out Hull Street. Its last car, No. 408 on the Hull Street–Highland Park run, ended Richmond's streetcars on 25 November 1949. The outer end is approximate.

features.name: Forest Hill line
features.route: 7th Street – Free Bridge – Semmes Avenue – Forest Hill Avenue
features.note: South over the river (the free bridge at Ninth Street), down the median of Semmes Avenue through Woodland Heights, and out Forest Hill Avenue to Forest Hill Park and its amusement park, the most popular trolley destination of all. VEPCO proposed taking up the Semmes Avenue tracks in 1933.

features.name: Richmond–Ashland Railway
features.route: Broad and Laurel – Brook Road – Ashland
features.note: The interurban to Ashland, built as the Richmond and Chesapeake Bay Railway (1907) and run as the Richmond–Ashland Railway from 1919 to 1938: from its terminal at Broad and Laurel Streets (814 West Broad), where the cars left from the second floor, north on a half-mile concrete viaduct over the Seaboard's tracks to just south of Brook Road (drawn straight, its line approximate), then beside Brook Road and on to Ashland on its own right-of-way.

rules.note: Little Westham Creek below Westhampton Lake is mapped underground (layer -1), in its culvert under the campus; drawn on the surface it ran under a building, so it is left out.
An unnamed stream east of Nine Mile Road whose mapped line runs along the slope above its ravine in the lidar, not in it: left out rather than drawn in the wrong place.
The streetcar company's Westhampton Park opened by the lake in May 1902.
Fountain (Boat) Lake is the pit dug for the berms of the New Reservoir, built 1875–1888.
Planned by 1914; by 1917 the park had its two new lakes.
Planned by 1914; by 1917 the park had its two new lakes.
The Diamond opened in April 1985 on the site of Parker Field (built in 1934 as part of the fair grounds, a ballpark from 1954).
The roundabout at the Seventh Street ramps of the I-64/I-95 interchange, part of the interstate's works: drawn today only (approximate, not sourced).
Settling basins, stormwater basins and pools: none is dated by a source here (the treatment plant's basins and the basins of the interstate's drainage among them), so they are drawn today only.
Basins: drawn today only, as above.
Treatment works and tanks: not dated here, drawn today only.
The unnamed ramps of the Manchester Bridge, dated with it.
The Boulevard's bridge over the RF&P by the fair grounds was built in 1943 (rebuilt 1986).
The Westwood Avenue bridges over the RF&P at AY (the avenue and its ramp, Saunders Avenue the other half of the pair) were built in 1966.
The other half of the 1966 Westwood Avenue bridges at AY (approximate: the bridge records name only Westwood Avenue and its ramp).
The loop ramp of the 1966 Westwood Avenue bridges.
Opened 1934 as a toll bridge (rebuilt 1985–88 on much the same line).
Approaches of the 1934 Lee Bridge (approximate: some may be older).
The Huguenot Memorial Bridge, opened 1950 (the low Westham Bridge of 1911 stood just by it).
Route 150 dates from 1967.
Opened 24 January 1973.
Opened 1 July 1958; designated I-95 a month later.
Opened 3 February 1976.
Unnamed ramps are dated with I-95.
The 9th Street (Manchester) Bridge was completed in 1973.

The curved link from 8th Street to Canal Street crosses ground that the USGS Richmond quadrangles of 1934 and 1956 show as rail yard, so it is later; when it was built is not known here, and it is drawn from 1957: approximate.
The bridge drawn is today's, of 1913. A bridge has stood near here since John Mayo Jr.'s toll bridge of 1788, but its earlier wooden spans are not drawn, so scenes before 1913 show no bridge here.
The floodwall was dedicated on 21 October 1994.
The canal's downtown end, from about 1800 until the railroad took it over (end date approximate); the stretch seen today was re-watered for the Canal Walk in 1999.
David Ross built the mill canal in 1790.

The Richmond and Petersburg (later Atlantic Coast Line) bridge over the James: rebuilt on concrete piers in 1902, removed in 1970. OSM keeps it as an abandoned railway, and today's scene (2026) draws it as OSM maps it, as before.

Lines out of use or taken up today: OSM does not say when they ran, and what is left of them are fragments that end in open ground or against later buildings (the spurs on the Manchester bank; the approach to the Church Hill Tunnel, which collapsed on 2 October 1925). Drawn in today's view only, unless a rule above dates one from a source.

The elevated viaducts and the Triple Crossing were built with Main Street Station, opened 1901. Rail bridges over the James (the Bellwood Subdivision and Richmond District crossings) are each one OSM way with their viaducts, so they are dated with them; no source here dates the river crossings themselves (undated: needs a source).
Railroads reach Richmond from 1836 (the RF&P); lines at grade are dated from then, although today's alignments are later.
Ramps and turning roads of the interchanges, dated with the turnpike: approximate, not sourced.
Parking aisles, driveways and drive-throughs, dated with surface parking (1960): approximate, not sourced.
Paths are not dated: drawn in today's view only.
Fountains are not dated: drawn in today's view only.
Surface parking, from 1960: the year by which the traced buildings no later map accounts for are assumed gone, when clearing for parking and highways began. Approximate, not sourced.
Road bridges not named above (over the rail lines and the interstate) are dated with the viaducts: approximate.
Roundabouts and traffic circles: the modern roundabout came to the United States in 1990, and those mapped here belong to the riverfront's redevelopment. Drawn from 1990: approximate.

Unnamed service roads of no particular kind (the drives and rings of parking lots, private drives): dated with surface parking, from 1960. Approximate, not sourced. Alleys (service=alley) and named service streets stay with the street grid.
The street grid is drawn in every year, within the town plan while it stands and, for minor streets, only beside a building of the year (streetsNearBuildings).
Any other way (construction, elevators, platforms): not dated, drawn today only.
Natural water courses are drawn in every year.

Dams, weirs, canals, drains and ditches not dated above (the Manchester Canal, the Hollywood and VEPCO dams among them): no source here dates them, so they are drawn today only. Undated: each needs a source.
Basins, ponds, pools and canal beds not dated above: drawn today only.
Piers, bridge outlines and other works: not dated, drawn today only.
Parks, playgrounds, sports fields and gardens: no source here dates them (Capitol Square, Libby Hill and Chimborazo parks among them), so they are drawn today only. Undated: each needs a source.
Cemeteries and laid-out grounds: no source here dates them (St. John's churchyard among them), so they are drawn today only. Undated: each needs a source.
Other amenities (fountains, plazas): not dated, drawn today only.

dates.name: South Falls garage
dates.note: The parking deck of the South Falls project, begun in 2018 (approximate).

dates.name: Greater Richmond Convention Center
dates.note: Today's building, the expansion of 2003, covering several blocks; the parcel's recorded year (1900) is an older building's.

dates.name: CarMax Park
dates.note: The Flying Squirrels' new ballpark, first played in in April 2026; the parcel's recorded year (1925) is an older building's.

dates.name: CarMax Park (grandstand)
dates.note: The Flying Squirrels' new ballpark, first played in in April 2026; the parcel's recorded year (1925) is an older building's.

dates.name: Sauer Center parking deck
dates.note: A five-level deck planned in May 2019 on the surface lot behind 2220 W. Broad Street; dated 2020 (approximate: built after the plan). The parcel's recorded year (1910) is an older building's.

dates.name: Cookie Factory tower
dates.note: The factory's first building, a six-storey tower completed in 1927; the company added to it through the 1940s and 1950s.

dates.name: Virginia Museum of Fine Arts
dates.note: Today's outline takes in the wings of 1954, 1970, 1976, 1984 and 2010 around the 1936 building facing the Boulevard. The 1936 building alone is not mapped, so the museum is not drawn before the outline was complete (approximate: it stood from 1936).

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol, central block
dates.note: Jefferson's Capitol, completed 1788 (https://vga.virginia.gov/?p=73). Its footprint is OSM's central building part (w366226948), taken to be the original building because it stands between the two wings of 1904–06; that identification is not from the source. OSM tags it 8.1 m; its height here, 26 m, is the roof height (85 ft, three floors) SkyscraperPage measured: https://skyscraperpage.com/b190890.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol, west wing
dates.note: One of the two wings added 1904–06, an OSM building part with two levels and no height (drawn about 7 m, below the houses around the square). 18 m, under the central block's 26 m roof, is approximate.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol, east wing
dates.note: One of the two wings added 1904–06, an OSM building part with two levels and no height (drawn about 7 m, below the houses around the square). 18 m, under the central block's 26 m roof, is approximate.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol
dates.note: The Capitol as OSM outlines it today, with the wings of 1904–06, from 1906. OSM maps it as three parts: the central block (below) and the two wings.

dates.name: St. John's Church
dates.note: Completed 1741 (https://lva-virginia.libguides.com/richmond-maps/history). A one-story frame church with a double-pitched roof, enlarged in 1772 and 1829, with a tower from 1833 (rebuilt 1866 and 1904–05). OSM gives no height, so it was drawn at the 16 m guess for a church; 9 m for the ridge is approximate. The outline is today's, so it shows the later additions in every year.

dates.name: First National Bank Building
dates.note: Completed 1913, Richmond's first high-rise; the assessor's year (1911) put it two years early.

dates.name: The Virginia
dates.note: Five-story apartment building of 1906 (National Register); the assessor's year (1847) is the parcel's, not the building's.

dates.name: Hotel John Marshall
dates.note: The hotel opened in 1929 (fifteen floors); the assessor's year (1920) put it in the 1925 scene.

dates.name: Riverside on the James
dates.note: The fifteen-story office tower was built in 2005; the assessor's year (1920) is the old power plant site's.

dates.name: Riverside on the James, parking deck
dates.note: The tower's attached parking deck. Its year is taken to be the tower's (2005); approximate.

dates.name: The Locks Tower
dates.note: Twelve-story apartment tower at 1001 E. Byrd St., completed by October 2019 (planned in 2017: https://richmondbizsense.com/2017/11/20/58m-12-story-tower-slated-along-canal/).

dates.name: South Falls Tower
dates.note: Fourteen-story L-shaped tower at 111 Hull St., finished in 2021 on a former paper-mill site; the assessor's year (1929) put it in the 1950 scene.

dates.name: The Hydro
dates.note: Seven-story apartment building at 101 Manchester Road, recently completed in April 2022.

dates.name: Shiplock Views
dates.note: New apartment building, five stories on Main Street and nine toward the river, slated to be finished in spring 2021.

dates.name: The Hues at City View
dates.note: Apartment building in Manchester completed in July 2025; the assessor's year (1920) put it in the 1925 scene.

dates.name: Virginia Mutual Building
dates.note: Built 1920–21 at 821 E. Main St. Curating its neighbor, the First National Bank Building, sets aside their shared parcel's year, so it is dated here.

dates.name: Ross Building
dates.note: The Ross Building, 801 E. Main St. (OSM: 8th and Main Apartments, old name Ross Building, 18 levels), finished in 1965: SkyscraperPage gives 1965 and 18 floors, and the Main Street Banking Historic District nomination of 2025 gives 1965 (16 stories): https://www.dhr.virginia.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/127-6031_Main_St_Banking_HD_2025_UpdateBD_NRHP_Nomination_FINAL.pdf. The assessor's year (1925) put the tower in the 1925 and 1950 scenes. What stood on the lot before is not known here, so earlier scenes leave the lot empty.

dates.name: Chesapeake and Potomac Telephone Company Building
dates.note: The C&P Telephone building at 703 E. Grace St. (OSM: Verizon Building), built in 1929 by Voorhees, Gmelin and Walker, with later additions. The assessor's year (1900) put it in the 1925 scene. Its building part (w365156597) takes this year.

dates.name: Federal Reserve Bank building (Supreme Court of Virginia)
dates.note: Built 1919–21 for the Federal Reserve Bank at 100 N. Ninth St.; the Supreme Court of Virginia since. The assessor's year is 1919.

dates.name: Hotel Richmond (Barbara Johns Building)
dates.note: The Hotel Richmond, later the Ninth Street Office Building: its first phase opened in 1904 and it was built out in phases until 1911; drawn whole from 1911. The assessor's year is 1903.

dates.name: Mutual Building
dates.note: 909 E. Main St.: built 1904, its upper floors added in 1912 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005); drawn at today's height from 1912. The assessor's year is 1904.

dates.name: Hotel Rueger (The Commonwealth)
dates.note: The Hotel Rueger at Ninth and Bank streets (later the Commonwealth Park Hotel), built 1912–13 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005; its entry is 9 N. Ninth St., OSM's 901 Bank St. is the same corner). The assessor's year is 1917.

dates.name: State and City Bank and Trust Company Building
dates.note: 900 E. Main St., fourteen stories, 1923 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005); the west tower of today's Pocahontas Building complex (https://historicrichmond.com/pocahontas-building/).

dates.name: Pocahontas Building, east tower
dates.note: The east tower of the Pocahontas Building complex at 900 E. Main St., added in 1962 (the 2005 district nomination lists it as a non-historic addition of 1962: https://www.dhr.virginia.gov/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/127-6031_Main_Street_Banking_HD_2005_NR_FINAL.pdf). The assessor's year (1923) is the west tower's.

dates.name: American National Bank Building
dates.note: 1001 E. Main St. (OSM: American Heritage Apartments), built 1904 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005). The assessor's year is 1910.

dates.name: 629 East Main Street
dates.note: Fourteen floors, completed 1922 (SkyscraperPage), as the assessor also gives.

dates.name: Virginia Electric and Power Company building (The Edison)
dates.note: 700 E. Franklin St., formerly the headquarters of Virginia Electric & Power Company, a high-rise built in 1913.

dates.name: Richmond Chamber of Commerce (Eskimo Pie) Building
dates.note: 530 E. Main St., built in 1912 for the Richmond Chamber of Commerce by Carneal and Johnston. The assessor's year is 1911.

dates.name: Richmond Garage
dates.note: The Richmond Garage at Sixth and Franklin streets, built in 1927: a parking garage that does date from before the decks of the 1960s (see parkingFrom).

dates.name: Upper Lofts at Canal Walk
dates.note: No source found for when this seven-level building was built: the listing's 1900 is the assessor's year, the only date there is, and is not taken. Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

dates.name: The Lofts at Shiplock Watch
dates.note: Richmond BizSense describes a three- and four-story building, so OSM's nine levels are wrong, and no source found gives its year (the assessor's is 1840). Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

dates.name: 501 East Franklin
dates.note: An eight-level building whose only date is the assessor's (1916); no other source found. Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

dates.name: Virginia Electric and Power Company building, annex
dates.note: The seven-story annex of the 1913 tower at 700 E. Franklin St.; no source found gives its year (the assessor's is the tower's lot, 1913). Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

dates.name: Grace Place Apartments
dates.note: The eleven-story apartment building at Grace and Fourth streets: no source found gives the year it was built (the assessor's 1922 is the lot's; its use as affordable housing dates from 2001). Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

A building part 45.7 m tall (OSM) whose only date is its parcel's (1890), far older than any building of that height downtown; no source found dates it. Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.
A building part 25 m tall (OSM) whose only date is its parcel's (1910); no source found dates it. Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.
